source.name: Stanford HAI
source.note: Definitions are paraphrased summaries of the terms listed on the source page. See the source for the original wording.

terms.definition: An attack in which someone covertly interferes with a model's training process.
terms.note: Source entry is cut off on the page.

terms.definition: A hypothetical AI system able to learn, reason, and apply knowledge across a broad range of tasks at or above human level.
AI systems that act as autonomous or semi-autonomous agents: they interpret goals, plan actions, use tools such as browsers, code, or APIs, and adjust based on feedback to finish tasks.
Ensuring an AI system's goals and behavior match human values, rules, and intentions.
Standardized tests used to measure and compare AI performance on tasks such as answering questions, recognizing images, coding, or following instructions.
The ability to work with AI productively and responsibly, combining practical tool skills, critical evaluation of outputs, ethical awareness, and adaptability as the technology changes.
The field concerned with making AI systems behave reliably and avoid causing harm, even when they are powerful, widely deployed, or facing unexpected situations.
An integrated set of software, hardware, and computing resources that supports the whole AI lifecycle.
terms.note: Source entry is cut off on the page.

terms.definition: The end-to-end process of building, deploying, and maintaining an AI system, from data collection through preparation, training, testing, and deployment.
A set of step-by-step instructions for solving a problem or completing a task, much like a recipe.
The situation where many organizations rely on the same or very similar AI programs, algorithms, or training data.
A network of AI systems or agents that share information and coordinate their actions.
terms.note: Source entry is cut off on the page.

terms.definition: A term coined in 1955 by John McCarthy, Stanford's first AI faculty member, for the science and engineering of making intelligent machines.
A neural network method that lets a model concentrate on the most relevant parts of its input when producing output.
Technology performing specific tasks according to explicit, predefined human instructions.
The way neural networks learn from errors, by working backward through the network to find which parts contributed to the mistake.
Graphical models that use probabilities to represent cause-and-effect relationships among variables.
When an AI system produces results that favor or discriminate against certain groups of people.
Datasets too large for traditional data-processing software, which AI can analyze to reveal patterns and trends.
A program designed to simulate conversation with people, usually by text or voice.
Also called proprietary software: software whose code is restricted and not available for the public to view, modify, or use.
A field of AI that lets computers see, identify, and interpret visual information from images and videos.
The amount of input, such as text, that an AI system can handle at one time during a task.
A technique where a model learns by comparing similar and dissimilar examples to understand what makes things alike or different.
Artificially enlarging a training dataset by creating modified versions of existing data rather than collecting new data.
Discovering patterns and trends in large datasets using statistical methods and machine learning.
An attack in which an adversary deliberately inserts, alters, or mislabels data in a model's training set.
terms.note: Source entry is cut off on the page.

terms.definition: An algorithm that predicts by asking a series of yes/no questions, splitting the data on features at each step until it reaches a conclusion.
A subset of machine learning that uses large multi-layer neural networks to learn complex patterns from data automatically.
Generative models that create new content, such as images, by adding noise and then removing it.
Simplifying complex data by cutting the number of variables while keeping the most important information.
Numerical vectors that represent complex data like words or images in a way that captures their meaning or characteristics.
Techniques that combine several models, often called weak learners, to get a more accurate and robust prediction than any single model.
Designing, building, and deploying AI in line with human values, fairness, transparency, and societal well-being.
AI programs that mimic human experts in a specific domain, using a knowledge base of facts and mainly if-then rules to reach conclusions.
Methods that make AI decisions and predictions understandable to humans instead of leaving them as opaque black boxes.
Training a model across many decentralized devices or servers that keep their data locally, so the data never leaves its original location.
An approach where models learn to handle new tasks from only a small number of examples.
Taking a pre-trained model and training it further on task- or domain-specific data.
terms.note: Source entry is cut off on the page.

terms.definition: Large models, often transformers, trained on vast and diverse data that can be adapted to many downstream tasks and applications.
A highly capable, general-purpose AI model at or near the leading edge of AI development.
AI systems that can create new content such as text, images, music, code, or video.
An architecture with two neural networks, a generator and a discriminator, that compete to produce realistic synthetic data.
A family of large language models built on the transformer architecture that generate human-like text from prompts.
A specialized chip, originally made for rendering graphics, that performs many mathematical calculations in parallel.
When an AI system produces incorrect, misleading, or fabricated information while presenting it as fact.
An approach to AI that puts human needs, values, and well-being first throughout development and deployment.
The ways in which people operate and engage with computer systems.
AI systems that build human feedback or intervention into how they operate.
A parameter whose value is set before a machine learning model begins learning.
A large technology company running vast data center networks that can rapidly scale computing, storage, and cloud services on demand.
When a trained AI model makes predictions or decisions on new data it has not seen before.
The degree to which humans can understand how an AI system reaches its decisions or predictions.
A simple, intuitive machine learning algorithm used for classification and regression.
A technique in which a smaller, simpler student model is trained to imitate the behavior and outputs of a larger model.
terms.note: Source entry is cut off on the page.

terms.definition: A structured database that represents information as a network of connected entities and their relationships.
An AI system trained on massive amounts of text to understand and generate human-like language.
A compressed, abstract space in which high-dimensional data is encoded into fewer dimensions while keeping its essential features and patterns.
The practice of managing the full lifecycle of LLM-based applications in production.
A mathematical measure, also called a cost or objective function, of how far a model's predictions are from the correct values.
A branch of AI in which computers learn patterns and make decisions from data without being explicitly programmed with rules.
A mathematical model of a sequence of events in which the probability of the next event depends only on the current state, not on past history.
Practices combining machine learning, software engineering, and DevOps to deploy, monitor, and maintain ML models reliably in production.
A simplified mathematical or computational representation of a real-world system, process, or relationship, used to make predictions or understand patterns.
A decline in a model's performance over time because real-world data has shifted away from the data it was trained on.
AI systems that can process, understand, and generate several types of data at once, such as text, images, audio, and video.
A branch of AI focused on letting computers understand, interpret, and generate human language meaningfully.
A computational model inspired by the brain, made of interconnected layers of artificial neurons that process and pass along information.
A method that improves a machine learning model by adjusting its settings so it makes fewer mistakes.
When a model memorizes its training data too closely, including errors and random patterns.
terms.note: Source entry is cut off on the page.

terms.definition: An AI model whose weights, code, training data (or an auditable account of it), and development tools are available to download, run, inspect, reproduce, modify, and improve.
An AI model whose core components are publicly released so anyone can download it.
Software whose original design, or blueprint, is freely available for anyone to see and use.
An internal variable in a machine learning model that is learned and adjusted during training.
Using data, statistics, and machine learning models to forecast future outcomes or trends.
Carefully crafting instructions, or prompts, to steer language models toward the desired outputs.
A security attack that uses malicious input to trick a large language model into behaving in unintended ways.
A technique that improves a language model's output by letting it look up external, current information first.
An AI system built to solve complex problems by producing a logical, step-by-step chain of thought.
A type of machine learning where an agent improves through trial and error by taking actions in a particular environment.
Frameworks, principles, and practices that guide the ethical and safe development and deployment of AI.
The field combining engineering and computer science, increasingly with AI, to design and build machines that perform physical tasks.
The ability to understand and reason about the three-dimensional physical world, including how objects relate, move, and interact in space.
A training method where a model creates its own puzzles from raw data and learns by solving them.
Understanding the meaning of language by examining relationships among words, phrases, and symbols.
Predictable mathematical relationships describing how model performance improves as model size, training data, and compute grow.
A machine learning approach where models are trained on labeled data, meaning inputs paired with correct outputs.
Artificially generated information produced by algorithms or simulations rather than collected from real-world events.
A container for numbers arranged in multiple dimensions, like a more advanced spreadsheet.
Breaking text into smaller units called tokens, such as words, word parts, or characters, that language models can process.
Earlier approaches to AI that relied on explicitly programmed rules, logic, and human-defined knowledge instead of learning from data.
The collection of examples, such as text, images, or audio, used to teach machine learning models how to do specific tasks.
Reusing a model trained on one task as the starting point for a different but related task.
A neural network architecture that uses attention to understand relationships among all parts of the input at once rather than sequentially.
A test proposed by Alan Turing in 1950 of whether a machine can show intelligent behavior indistinguishable from a human's.
A machine learning approach where models work on data without labels or predefined categories and must find patterns and structure themselves.
A specialized database designed to store and efficiently search high-dimensional vector representations of data like text, images, or audio.
An adaptation of the transformer architecture, originally built for language, to process and analyze images.
The numerical parameters in a neural network that set the strength of connections between artificial neurons and shape how the model processes information.
A model's ability to perform tasks or recognize categories it was never explicitly trained on, relying on its general knowledge.
